vignette:
Tane is a 53-year-old airline pilot who had spent most of his adult life priding himself on calm judgment, disciplined routines, and the ability to function under pressure. During a period overseas several years ago, he was detained and tortured. He does not recount it in a flowing story. What comes back are fixed images: a metal door, a narrow room packed too close with bodies and heat, the face of a guard leaning in while someone nearby cried, the sour smell of sweat and damp concrete. He remembers men being humiliated and beaten for the smallest perceived infraction, and what stayed with him most was not only the pain and fear but the sense that ordinary rules had vanished, that people could behave with deliberate cruelty and call it justified. Even now, when he approaches the memory, it arrives as stark snapshots rather than a narrative, and the smell comes with it so vividly that for a moment he feels he is back inside that room. If he lets it go on too long, the emotion surges so strongly that he has to shut it down.

In the months after he returned home to the United States, Tane found that certain moments in ordinary life hit him with a force he could not explain to anyone around him. Crowded places were the worst. Walking through an airport concourse, standing in a packed shuttle bus, or waiting in a tightly bunched security line could abruptly make his chest tighten, not just from the press of people but from the sense of being trapped among bodies again. Seeing someone cry, even briefly, could stop him cold. What also set him off was witnessing people act badly in public—an angry passenger berating a gate agent, someone shoving ahead in line, a stranger behaving with arrogant disregard. In those moments, it was as if the world had tilted back toward the same lawless cruelty he had seen during detention. He became sharply watchful, scanning faces and movements around him for signs that someone might turn dangerous.

The triggers did not stay confined to the moment. A crying child in a terminal or a crowd closing in at boarding would often pull up those visual fragments with brutal immediacy: the room, the faces, the door. At times he could smell the air from captivity so distinctly that he would step away from others and steady himself against a wall, embarrassed by how completely his mind had been overtaken. Because the memory came in photographic flashes and quickly became overwhelming, he learned to cut it off as fast as possible, but that left him braced and vigilant for the rest of the day. The memory itself had come to feel like a warning signal. When those images and smells broke through, he took them as evidence that danger was near and that he could not afford to relax.

Over time that sense of threat spread into his home and work life. Silence, especially unusual silence, became difficult to bear. If the house was too still at night, he would feel a sick certainty that something was about to happen. He made repeated rounds checking locks and windows, sometimes returning to the same door minutes later despite knowing he had already secured it. He watched other people closely, including strangers in terminals and, to his wife’s distress, even neighbors or service workers who had done nothing overtly wrong. His threat monitoring also fed back into what provoked him. In any crowded place he was no longer simply among people; he was studying who looked agitated, who seemed disrespectful, who might suddenly lash out. That constant scanning made public conflict and misbehavior stand out instantly, and once he noticed one crying person or one pushing, angry passenger, the whole environment became charged.

As an airline pilot, he could not avoid airports, boarding areas, and tightly managed public spaces. He began altering his routines in small but consequential ways—arriving through quieter entrances when possible, lingering in restricted crew areas, choosing routes through terminals that minimized contact with dense crowds. Even so, a gate area filling with impatient passengers or the sound of someone crying nearby could set the whole sequence in motion: the flash of images, the remembered smell, the conviction that he needed to watch everyone, the urge to get somewhere he could check an exit. The more he lived this way, the more potent those cues became. He had come to expect that crowds, tears, and public disrespect meant threat, and because he was already on guard for them, he found them everywhere.

By the time he sought help, his world had narrowed despite the fact that he was still working. His wife had grown frustrated with the nightly checking and with how absent he became in public, his eyes always moving, his attention captured by who might be unsafe. What frightened Tane most was not simply remembering what had happened, but the sense that the memory could be summoned by almost anything and that once it arrived he was no longer fully in the present. He came to treatment after realizing that even in the familiar silence of his own home, and even in the routine environment of the airport where he had once felt most competent, he was living as if danger were about to break through at any moment. He says he wants, more than anything, to be able to move through a crowd and hear quiet without waiting for the next sign that something terrible is about to begin again.
